task.goal: Create a low-pressure way for a repair café to celebrate failed repair attempts as useful learning rather than shame.
hard_constraints: Four volunteers have a table, paper and a small display board for one monthly event.
No photos or names without explicit consent, no prizes or leaderboards, and no unsafe repair advice.
Participation is optional, usable without public speaking, and does not slow the queue substantially; pilot with observation and opt-out checks.
task.available_resources: Existing repair notes with permission to summarize anonymously.
task.expected_result: A concrete ritual and evaluation of learning versus embarrassment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Useful Ending
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make an unsuccessful repair produce a small, optional learning record. The mechanism is to give the attempt a useful endpoint: an observation or boundary worth remembering, even when the item remains broken.

At handback, a volunteer offers a paper slip: “Still broken; now we know…” The owner can tick “one possibility ruled out,” “a limit identified,” “a question clarified,” or “nothing clear yet,” then optionally add a sentence. No explanation aloud is required. Blank slips are fine. The owner keeps the slip unless they separately consent to an anonymous summary appearing on the board. A volunteer reviews any shared wording, removing identifying details and procedural repair advice. The board heading reads “Useful endings this month.” Permitted existing notes can supply a few examples without implying that their owners joined this ritual.

Four volunteers use one table corner for slips and the small board for summaries. The handback volunteer makes the offer; another reviews contributions during quiet moments. Folding paper creates separate collection pockets for publication consent and private feedback. Participation should take under a minute away from the service queue.

This assumes some visitors value a concrete record of what changed. It may feel forced when nothing useful emerged, so “nothing clear yet” must remain an equally acceptable ending. The ritual celebrates careful inquiry without claiming every failure is beneficial.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate short handback periods offering either an ordinary repair summary or that summary plus the optional slip. In both periods, offer anonymous exit ticks: “I learned something useful: yes/unsure/no” and “The handback made me feel embarrassed or pressured: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes handback time and whether declined offers are accepted immediately, without recording identities. Inspect whether completed slips contain a specific observation rather than compulsory positivity. The idea is weakened if learning responses resemble the comparator while embarrassment, pressure, or delays increase. Low response numbers and self-selection limit conclusions; do not treat uptake as proof of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Open Questions Board
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Celebrate failed attempts by treating them as contributions to the café’s shared understanding of uncertainty. The mechanism is collective sense-making: an unresolved item can reveal a recurring question worth investigating, without putting its owner on display.

Before the event, volunteers turn permitted repair notes into three or four anonymous, non-procedural questions, such as “What information was missing before diagnosis?” or “When did we recognize that this repair exceeded our facilities?” Each card includes an honest statement of what remains unknown. Avoid item descriptions that could identify someone.

Visitors may silently read the board, place a pencil mark beside a question that helped them understand their own visit, or submit a new question on paper. Nothing requires describing their repair publicly. New submissions need a separate publication-consent tick and volunteer review. The closing ritual is a handwritten board footer: “These questions are worth carrying forward,” followed by one or two questions selected for relevance and safe scope, without vote totals or rankings. No promise of a future answer is made.

One volunteer prepares the initial cards, one checks proposed additions during quiet periods, and all four continue their ordinary repair roles. Reading and marking happen at the table edge after handback, outside the queue.

This assumes shared uncertainty can reduce isolation and support learning. It could instead resemble a catalogue of inadequacy or invite speculative technical advice. Keep all cards about observations, information needs, and service limits; omit repair instructions and unsupported explanations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Display the same permitted note summaries first as plain anonymous accounts and then as open questions, switching order midway through the event if practical. Offer separate optional paper responses: “What, if anything, did this help you understand?” and “Did this display make failed repairs feel more acceptable, unchanged, or more uncomfortable?” Observe congestion and whether visitors can bypass it easily. Compare the specificity of learning responses and reported discomfort between versions. The mechanism is doubtful if questions generate only vague approval, greater discomfort, or unsafe advice submissions. Different visitors and time periods make this a small design check, not causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Thank the Care, Leave the Outcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a private acknowledgment ritual to separate appreciation of a repair attempt from whether it succeeded. The mechanism is relational: a visitor can feel respected when someone recognizes a specific act of care, without having to reinterpret disappointment as success.

At handback, a volunteer may offer a folded paper card: “Would you like a short acknowledgment of the attempt? Passing is fine.” Inside, the volunteer writes one truthful, observable contribution, such as “You explained the fault clearly” or “We stopped when we reached the limits of our equipment.” Avoid praising persistence indiscriminately, assigning blame, or implying that stopping proves a repair was safe. The visitor can keep, decline, or discard it without explanation. There is no public reading.

A separate optional slip asks, “What care or effort would you like this café to recognize?” Visitors may acknowledge listening, patience, clear explanations, or respecting a decision to stop. With explicit permission, volunteers summarize these themes anonymously on the board under “Care we noticed today.” The board contains neither identifiable repair stories nor individual credits. This makes celebration visible while keeping personal acknowledgment private.

Four volunteers agree on a few factual wording examples before opening. Cards are completed only when handback allows; otherwise a visitor can take a blank reflection card to the table. One volunteer checks board contributions during a lull. Existing notes are unnecessary.

The approach assumes recognition feels supportive. It may seem patronizing, especially after a frustrating visit, and it does not itself establish technical learning. The offer must be brief, sincere, and easy to refuse.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare ordinary handbacks with handbacks offering the private acknowledgment during alternating short periods. Give both groups optional anonymous exit questions: “I felt respected,” “I can name something learned or a limit clarified,” and “I felt expected to be positive,” each with yes/unsure/no options. Observe added handback time, repeated offers after refusal, and any queue obstruction. A useful result would combine respect with identifiable learning or clearer limits, without increased pressure. Reject or revise the ritual if appreciation rises but pressure also rises, or if visitors describe it as patronizing. Sparse feedback leaves uncertainty; silence and acceptance are not evidence of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Volunteers Go First
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible before inviting any visitor contribution. The mechanism is norm-setting through example: when the people treated as experts acknowledge uncertainty and disappointment without self-mockery, visitors may feel less personally judged by an unsuccessful repair.

Before opening, each willing volunteer writes a short anonymous account of an attempt they personally made: “We hoped… / What happened… / What changed in our understanding…” Use only truthful accounts they consent to share. Include unresolved disappointment where appropriate; do not manufacture a lesson. Exclude identifying item details, repair instructions, and claims that an item is safe. Two accounts are enough if others prefer to pass.

Display these under “Our attempts sometimes end here too.” At handback, a volunteer can briefly point out that the board is optional reading, without asking the visitor to contribute or respond. Beside it, provide folded paper headed “Something I wish repair volunteers understood about an unsuccessful visit.” Visitors can deposit an anonymous private note without speaking. These notes remain private and are not added to the display.

During a quiet moment near closing, the four volunteers read the notes and write one collective acknowledgment on the board, such as “A disappointing outcome can still deserve a clear explanation.” This closes the ritual without displaying visitors’ experiences or requiring positive feelings.

The table, paper, and board suffice; preparation takes a few minutes, and reading happens beyond the queue. The approach assumes volunteer examples feel credible and relatable. It could instead undermine confidence or make visitors feel responsible for comforting volunteers. Keep accounts brief, avoid excuses, and never seek reassurance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot during one event with alternating display periods: a neutral description of the café’s repair limits versus the volunteer accounts. Offer the same optional anonymous exit slip in both periods: “An unsuccessful repair would make me feel judged here: yes/unsure/no”; “Something this helped me understand: ___”; and “I felt asked to reassure volunteers: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes queue obstruction and whether people can bypass the display and decline feedback without another invitation. Revise or stop if the accounts increase reported judgment, solicit comforting responses, or produce reassurance without identifiable learning. Different visitors, timing, and voluntary responses prevent a causal conclusion; uptake alone does not show comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Failed Attempt Changes Our Welcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give unsuccessful attempts a concrete consequence in how the café operates. The mechanism is visible institutional responsiveness: an attempt becomes useful because the café changes a small practice in response, rather than asking its owner to find a positive meaning in the outcome.

Before the event, volunteers review existing repair notes that may be summarized anonymously. Choose one recurring, well-supported communication problem associated with unsuccessful visits—for example, visitors not knowing which equipment the café lacks. Do not infer a recurring problem from a single ambiguous note. Agree on one modest change achievable with paper, such as placing a plain-language facilities notice at the table.

Put a two-part card on the display board: “Earlier unsuccessful attempts showed us…” and “Today we changed…” Describe the communication gap and actual change without identifying visitors, blaming anyone, or giving technical repair advice. Label it “An attempt that changed the café.” This is the celebratory act: publicly crediting unsuccessful work with improving the service, without naming its participants or suggesting their disappointment was necessary.

After handback, anyone may silently leave a private slip completing “One thing that would have made today clearer…” Submission is optional and separate from service. A publication-consent box permits an anonymous summary, but private feedback remains useful without that permission. During a lull, volunteers may implement one feasible clarification and update the board only after doing so. If nothing suitable emerges, leave the original change visible rather than inventing progress.

All four volunteers retain their repair roles; one checks slips during quiet periods. This requires authority to make small communication changes and enough permitted notes to identify a genuine issue. It cannot compensate for a poor repair explanation, and the board could feel promotional unless it states the change modestly and honestly.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For a small prototype, alternate between displaying the new facilities notice alone and displaying it with the anonymous account of why it changed. Keep the actual service improvement available throughout. Offer optional exit ticks: “I understand this café’s limits”; “Unsuccessful attempts seem useful to improving this café”; and “This framing made my disappointment feel dismissed,” each with yes/unsure/no, plus space for an example of something learned. Observe congestion, unobstructed opt-out, and whether volunteers pursue declined feedback. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the origin story adds no understanding or usefulness, or increases dismissal. Inspect whether the promised change actually happened. One event provides a practical design check, with substantial uncertainty from small numbers and self-selection.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Hindsight Fold
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Turn a permitted account of an unsuccessful repair into a silent, folded-paper exercise that lets visitors experience how uncertainty changes with information. The mechanism is perspective-taking: an outcome can look obvious afterward, while an honest reconstruction shows why the attempt was informative.

Before the event, two volunteers select one existing repair note with permission for anonymous summarization. It must document both an initial uncertainty and something the attempt actually established. If no note supports that sequence, do not manufacture one. Remove identifying details and all procedural repair advice.

The outside of a folded sheet gives the initial situation in broad terms and asks: “Could you tell whether a repair would be possible from this information?” Readers can privately consider “yes,” “no,” or “unsure,” without submitting an answer. Inside, reveal the documented outcome and the specific information gained. Include “The item remained unrepaired” plainly. The final line reads: “This attempt gave us a case worth learning from. Disappointment can remain.” There is no correct-answer score, public response, or invitation to diagnose the item.

Place a few copies at the table edge, clear of the queue. The board holds the same folded case under “An unsuccessful attempt, a useful lesson.” Opening the fold is the optional ritual; visitors need neither speak nor contribute their own experience. Two volunteers prepare and check the wording before opening; all four retain their ordinary roles during service.

This assumes the notes preserve enough information to reconstruct uncertainty faithfully. A selective account could excuse poor work or exaggerate learning. Use modest claims and omit cases whose educational value depends on technical instructions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate the folded version with an unfolded version containing exactly the same account. Offer optional anonymous slips asking: “What did this attempt establish?”, “Did this make unsuccessful repairs feel less shameful, unchanged, or more shameful?”, and “Did you feel tested or pressured?” Observe obstruction and whether visitors can ignore the display without prompting. Stop or revise if the fold attracts guessing but yields no clearer learning, increases embarrassment, or delays service. Sparse, self-selected feedback cannot establish effectiveness; inspect unanswered and critical responses alongside favorable ones.

EXPAND.title: The Volunteers Go First
EXPAND.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible so visitors encounter fallibility as an ordinary part of skilled work. The mechanism is modeling: people may feel less personally judged when helpers openly acknowledge their own uncertainty and mistakes.

Before opening, two volunteers each prepare a short, truthful account of an unsuccessful attempt involving their own belongings, or an account they have explicit permission to share anonymously. Each follows three prompts: “What I expected,” “What the attempt actually showed,” and “What I would notice earlier next time.” Include only supported observations, without repair procedures, identifying details, or claims that an unresolved item is safe.

Put these accounts on the small board under “Our attempts don’t always work either.” The monthly ritual is for volunteers to add one honest learning sentence before the doors open. Visitors can read silently or bypass the display; nobody asks them to contribute their own failure. A paper footer says, “Disappointment is welcome here too.” This celebrates helpers’ willingness to learn without requiring owners to feel grateful about a broken item.

Two volunteers supply accounts, a third checks accuracy and privacy, and the fourth checks that the display is readable from outside the queue. Preparation needs paper and a brief discussion; no volunteer remains stationed at the board.

This assumes volunteers can share credible examples without turning them into heroic stories. Self-deprecating jokes, exaggerated incompetence, or accounts that quietly blame owners could undermine trust. If suitable accounts are unavailable, do not invent them. Reading a display also cannot establish that visitors have learned anything transferable.
EXPAND.experiment: For two short periods, show either the volunteer accounts or a plain explanation of the café’s repair limits, alternating their order once. Offer optional anonymous paper ticks about useful learning, embarrassment, and confidence in the helpers, plus an optional sentence naming something learned. One volunteer observes obstruction and checks that bypassing visitors receive no further invitation. Revise or reject the display if it increases discomfort or weakens confidence without producing specific learning. Small, self-selected responses cannot establish a reliable effect.

EXPAND.title: The Next-Time Choice
EXPAND.proposal:
Turn an unsuccessful attempt into a short opportunity to rehearse a useful decision. The mechanism is active application: visitors try using a lesson in a different situation, rather than merely reading that a lesson exists.

Using existing notes permitted for anonymous summarization, volunteers prepare two paper cases. Each describes an unsuccessful attempt and a documented information gap or service limit. Remove distinctive item details. Follow each case with a nontechnical choice, such as: “Before another visit, what would help most: record when the fault occurs, assume a cause, or leave the description blank?” Under a folded flap, explain why an observation could help while explicitly saying that it does not guarantee repair. Include “There isn’t enough information” wherever that is the honest answer.

The board reads “An attempt we can learn with.” The ritual is a silent choose-and-reveal moment at the table after handback. Visitors may point privately, think without marking anything, or skip it. Their own repair is never the exercise. There are no scores, correct-answer totals, prizes, or requests to demonstrate competence aloud.

One volunteer drafts the cases, another verifies that the lessons follow from the notes, a third checks for identifying details and unsafe implications, and the fourth places the materials away from the queue. All return to ordinary duties. Cards stay within observation, communication, and café boundaries; they contain no instructions for opening, powering, or testing equipment.

The prerequisite is at least one note with a defensible lesson. The limits are accessibility and tone: a quiz-like presentation could feel childish or evaluative. Use adult language, large writing, and an explicit invitation to ignore the exercise.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare one folded choice case with a plain card containing the same case and explanation. Optional anonymous feedback asks visitors to apply the lesson to one different, equally safe example and report whether the format felt helpful, embarrassing, or like a test. Observe bypasses and table congestion without tracking individuals. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the choice version produces no clearer application than ordinary reading, or adds embarrassment. A few successful answers show feasibility, not lasting learning.

EXPAND.title: One Attempt Changes the Café
EXPAND.proposal:
Celebrate unsuccessful attempts through a small change to how the café works. The mechanism is institutional responsiveness: a failed repair becomes useful because the organization acts on a supported lesson, rather than asking its owner to supply a positive interpretation.

Before the event, review permitted repair notes for one recurring, nontechnical service issue that contributed to an unproductive attempt. Examples could include an unclear description of available facilities or a missed opportunity to ask when a fault occurs. Only choose an issue supported by the notes and a change achievable with paper during this event.

Write a three-part board card: “An attempt revealed…,” “Today we are trying…,” and “We still don’t know….” For example, an unsuccessful diagnosis might motivate an optional written prompt about when a problem appears. Do not imply that the change will make repairs succeed. Remove identifying details and omit unsafe repair advice.

The ritual is a short, quiet opening action: the volunteers place the revised prompt or clarification into use and turn the board card from “proposed” to “trying today.” Visitors can silently leave a paper comment or ignore the display. Contributions about personal experiences remain private unless separately approved for anonymous publication. No individual receives credit or blame.

The four volunteers divide note review, drafting, privacy checking, and observation, then resume their usual roles. The change must fit existing handbacks or optional paperwork rather than create another queue stage.

This assumes a modest service improvement is available and volunteers can implement it consistently. The board must not advertise a speculative improvement as an achieved result. A lesson may concern café organization rather than repair technique; that still counts, but should be described honestly.
EXPAND.experiment: Try the revised prompt during one short period and use the ordinary process during another. Inspect whether the specific problem identified in the notes occurs less often, while recording approximate added time and optional anonymous learning and embarrassment ticks. Observe whether declined prompts are immediately dropped. Withdraw the change if it adds friction without addressing the problem, or makes visitors feel responsible for improving the café. Sparse observations support a local revision, not a claim that failed repairs generally improve services.

EXPAND.title: Room for an Unfinished Ending
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce shame by changing the expectation visitors bring to a repair attempt. The mechanism is expectation calibration: an unresolved outcome may feel less like personal failure when it was presented beforehand as a legitimate possibility with its own useful forms of closure.

At the table, place a plain paper card headed “What today might provide.” Give equal visual space to three possibilities: “A repair,” “A clearer observation or limit,” and “Still unresolved.” Add: “You do not have to call an unsuccessful visit a success.” Visitors may read it silently; staff do not ask them to choose or predict an outcome.

At handback, use the ordinary factual explanation. An optional take-away strip repeats the three possibilities and says, “An unfinished attempt belongs here too.” The monthly celebration is a board heading, “We make room for unfinished work,” accompanied by one or two permitted anonymous examples showing different endings. Include an example where nothing clear was learned if the notes support one. Do not publish visitor names, photographs, identifiable cases, or new contributions without explicit consent.

One volunteer drafts the card, another checks that the examples accurately reflect the notes, a third checks privacy and safety, and the fourth checks placement outside the moving queue. No additional conversation or dedicated station is required.

This assumes some embarrassment comes from expecting every competent attempt to end in a repair. It will help less when distress comes from cost, attachment, or an unpleasant interaction. It could also sound like an excuse for poor service. Keep wording specific to uncertainty, maintain normal care, and avoid presenting every unsuccessful attempt as educational.
EXPAND.experiment: During alternating arrival periods, display either this outcomes card or a similarly sized card explaining ordinary event logistics. Both periods receive the same optional anonymous exit questions: “Did your visit provide useful learning?”, “Did the outcome feel personally embarrassing?”, and “Did the café seem to excuse avoidable problems?” Observe queue movement and whether visitors can bypass all materials without follow-up. The approach is weakened if embarrassment stays unchanged, learning declines, or visitors perceive lowered standards. Differences between arrival groups and voluntary feedback leave substantial uncertainty.

EXPAND.title: Judge the Attempt Before the Ending
EXPAND.proposal:
Make a monthly ritual of recognizing a well-conducted attempt before revealing whether it succeeded. The mechanism is correcting outcome bias: people can mistake a broken item for evidence that its owner or helper did something foolish. Separating process from outcome may make room for disappointment alongside justified appreciation.

Prepare two clearly labeled fictional examples on paper. Both describe the same nontechnical conduct: the owner explained the problem, the volunteer acknowledged uncertainty, and they respected the café’s limits. Fold each ending underneath: one item worked again; the other remained unresolved. Do not include diagnostic procedures or imply that either item is safe to use.

The board invites: “Before opening the endings, notice what deserves appreciation in both attempts.” Visitors can silently read, unfold the endings, and consider: “Does the ending change which actions were worthwhile?” There are no answers to submit or scores. A closing strip reads: “Careful attempts deserve acknowledgment. Unsuccessful outcomes still deserve honest explanations.” The monthly ritual is replacing the example pair, rather than collecting visitors’ failures.

One volunteer drafts, another checks that the stories differ only in outcome, a third reviews safety and tone, and the fourth observes the pilot. All retain their normal roles; the paper sits at the table edge outside the queue. No names or photos are collected, and no personal account is displayed without explicit consent.

This assumes some shame comes from judging competence solely by results. It cannot resolve financial loss or attachment to an item. Fictional examples may also feel artificial or excuse poor service; the wording must preserve accountability for actual mistakes.
EXPAND.experiment: During two short observation periods, alternate the folded pair with a simple comparator card saying, “Unsuccessful repairs are welcome here.” Offer the same optional private feedback slip in both periods: “One thing this helped me understand,” “Did this feel reassuring, embarrassing, judgmental, or neither?” and “Was it easy to skip?” Include “prefer not to answer.” Observe queue obstruction and whether volunteers repeatedly prompt participation; do not record identities or infer feelings from expressions. The mechanism is weakened if readers cannot explain why process and outcome deserve separate judgments, or describe the pair as patronizing or an excuse. Remove it if opting out attracts attention or it disrupts service. Small, self-selected responses provide a usability check, not proof of reduced shame.

With explicit permission, volunteers summarize these themes anonymously on the board under “Care we noticed today.” The board contains neither identifiable repair stories nor individual credits. This makes celebration visible while keeping personal acknowledgment private.

Four volunteers agree on a few factual wording examples before opening. Cards are completed only when handback allows; otherwise a visitor can take a blank reflection card to the table. One volunteer checks board contributions during a lull. Existing notes are unnecessary.

The approach assumes recognition feels supportive. It may seem patronizing, especially after a frustrating visit, and it does not itself establish technical learning. The offer must be brief, sincere, and easy to refuse.
REFINE.experiment: Compare ordinary handbacks with handbacks offering the private acknowledgment during alternating short periods. Give both groups optional anonymous exit questions: “I felt respected,” “I can name something learned or a limit clarified,” and “I felt expected to be positive,” each with yes/unsure/no options. Observe added handback time, repeated offers after refusal, and any queue obstruction. A useful result would combine respect with identifiable learning or clearer limits, without increased pressure. Reject or revise the ritual if appreciation rises but pressure also rises, or if visitors describe it as patronizing. Sparse feedback leaves uncertainty; silence and acceptance are not evidence of comfort.

REFINE.title: Volunteers Go First
REFINE.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible before inviting any visitor contribution. The mechanism is norm-setting through example: when the people treated as experts acknowledge uncertainty and disappointment without self-mockery, visitors may feel less personally judged by an unsuccessful repair.

Before opening, each willing volunteer writes a short anonymous account of an attempt they personally made: “We hoped… / What happened… / What changed in our understanding…” Use only truthful accounts they consent to share. Include unresolved disappointment where appropriate; do not manufacture a lesson. Exclude identifying item details, repair instructions, and claims that an item is safe. Two accounts are enough if others prefer to pass.

Display these under “Our attempts sometimes end here too.” At handback, a volunteer can briefly point out that the board is optional reading, without asking the visitor to contribute or respond. Beside it, provide folded paper headed “Something I wish repair volunteers understood about an unsuccessful visit.” Visitors can deposit an anonymous private note without speaking. These notes remain private and are not added to the display.

During a quiet moment near closing, the four volunteers read the notes and write one collective acknowledgment on the board, such as “A disappointing outcome can still deserve a clear explanation.” This closes the ritual without displaying visitors’ experiences or requiring positive feelings.

The table, paper, and board suffice; preparation takes a few minutes, and reading happens beyond the queue. The approach assumes volunteer examples feel credible and relatable. It could instead undermine confidence or make visitors feel responsible for comforting volunteers. Keep accounts brief, avoid excuses, and never seek reassurance.
REFINE.experiment: Pilot during one event with alternating display periods: a neutral description of the café’s repair limits versus the volunteer accounts. Offer the same optional anonymous exit slip in both periods: “An unsuccessful repair would make me feel judged here: yes/unsure/no”; “Something this helped me understand: ___”; and “I felt asked to reassure volunteers: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes queue obstruction and whether people can bypass the display and decline feedback without another invitation. Revise or stop if the accounts increase reported judgment, solicit comforting responses, or produce reassurance without identifiable learning. Different visitors, timing, and voluntary responses prevent a causal conclusion; uptake alone does not show comfort.

REFINE.title: A Failed Attempt Changes Our Welcome
REFINE.proposal:
Give unsuccessful attempts a concrete consequence in how the café operates. The mechanism is visible institutional responsiveness: an attempt becomes useful because the café changes a small practice in response, rather than asking its owner to find a positive meaning in the outcome.

Before the event, volunteers review existing repair notes that may be summarized anonymously. Choose one recurring, well-supported communication problem associated with unsuccessful visits—for example, visitors not knowing which equipment the café lacks. Do not infer a recurring problem from a single ambiguous note. Agree on one modest change achievable with paper, such as placing a plain-language facilities notice at the table.

Put a two-part card on the display board: “Earlier unsuccessful attempts showed us…” and “Today we changed…” Describe the communication gap and actual change without identifying visitors, blaming anyone, or giving technical repair advice. Label it “An attempt that changed the café.” This is the celebratory act: publicly crediting unsuccessful work with improving the service, without naming its participants or suggesting their disappointment was necessary.

After handback, anyone may silently leave a private slip completing “One thing that would have made today clearer…” Submission is optional and separate from service. A publication-consent box permits an anonymous summary, but private feedback remains useful without that permission. During a lull, volunteers may implement one feasible clarification and update the board only after doing so. If nothing suitable emerges, leave the original change visible rather than inventing progress.

All four volunteers retain their repair roles; one checks slips during quiet periods. This requires authority to make small communication changes and enough permitted notes to identify a genuine issue. It cannot compensate for a poor repair explanation, and the board could feel promotional unless it states the change modestly and honestly.
REFINE.experiment: For a small prototype, alternate between displaying the new facilities notice alone and displaying it with the anonymous account of why it changed. Keep the actual service improvement available throughout. Offer optional exit ticks: “I understand this café’s limits”; “Unsuccessful attempts seem useful to improving this café”; and “This framing made my disappointment feel dismissed,” each with yes/unsure/no, plus space for an example of something learned. Observe congestion, unobstructed opt-out, and whether volunteers pursue declined feedback. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the origin story adds no understanding or usefulness, or increases dismissal. Inspect whether the promised change actually happened. One event provides a practical design check, with substantial uncertainty from small numbers and self-selection.

REFINE.title: A Useful Ending, Without Homework
REFINE.proposal:
Repair original candidate 0, the strongest fit because it gives an unsuccessful attempt a useful endpoint with little equipment or ceremony. Its specific weakness is asking a disappointed visitor to classify or invent a lesson at handback: that can turn recognition into homework and imply that leaving without a lesson is another failure.

Change only who supplies the learning record. When the ordinary repair explanation establishes a concrete observation or limit, the volunteer writes that fact on a small take-away slip: “Still unresolved. Today we established: ___.” If nothing was established, write “Still unresolved; no clear finding today.” Offer it once: “You can take this summary or leave it.” No visitor completion or spoken response is needed. Do not claim a cause was ruled out unless the repair notes support it, or include procedures or safety assurances.

Keep the original optional board mechanism: the visitor may separately tick explicit permission for an anonymous summary, reviewed during a lull. Give honest uncertainty equal standing under “Useful endings this month,” without requiring a positive lesson. Four volunteers retain their repair roles; one reviews slips when free, and the table corner holds paper outside the queue.

Prerequisites are a factual ordinary handback summary and agreement on brief, non-procedural wording. Permitted existing notes can seed anonymous examples. The remaining limit is that a written finding may still feel patronizing, and receiving it does not demonstrate learning.
REFINE.experiment: For one monthly event, alternate short periods of ordinary handbacks and handbacks with the prepared-slip offer. In both periods, provide optional anonymous exit paper: “One thing I now understand, if anything: ___”; “I felt expected to find a positive lesson: yes/unsure/no”; and “I felt embarrassed by the handback: yes/unsure/no.” Mark the period on the paper without recording identities. A volunteer tallies added handback time, queue obstruction, and whether every refusal ends the offer immediately. The smallest falsifying result is visitors reporting pressure to find a lesson despite the prepared wording, or observations that writing slips repeatedly delays the queue. Compare concrete understanding and discomfort across periods; small, self-selected responses support revision, not a causal claim.

SAVE.title: A Useful Ending
SAVE.proposal:
Make an unsuccessful repair produce a small, optional learning record. The mechanism is to give the attempt a useful endpoint: an observation or boundary worth remembering, even when the item remains broken.

At handback, a volunteer offers a paper slip: “Still broken; now we know…” The owner can tick “one possibility ruled out,” “a limit identified,” “a question clarified,” or “nothing clear yet,” then optionally add a sentence. No explanation aloud is required. Blank slips are fine. The owner keeps the slip unless they separately consent to an anonymous summary appearing on the board. A volunteer reviews any shared wording, removing identifying details and procedural repair advice. The board heading reads “Useful endings this month.” Permitted existing notes can supply a few examples without implying that their owners joined this ritual.

Four volunteers use one table corner for slips and the small board for summaries. The handback volunteer makes the offer; another reviews contributions during quiet moments. Folding paper creates separate collection pockets for publication consent and private feedback. Participation should take under a minute away from the service queue.

This assumes some visitors value a concrete record of what changed. It may feel forced when nothing useful emerged, so “nothing clear yet” must remain an equally acceptable ending. The ritual celebrates careful inquiry without claiming every failure is beneficial.
SAVE.experiment: During one event, alternate short handback periods offering either an ordinary repair summary or that summary plus the optional slip. In both periods, offer anonymous exit ticks: “I learned something useful: yes/unsure/no” and “The handback made me feel embarrassed or pressured: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes handback time and whether declined offers are accepted immediately, without recording identities. Inspect whether completed slips contain a specific observation rather than compulsory positivity. The idea is weakened if learning responses resemble the comparator while embarrassment, pressure, or delays increase. Low response numbers and self-selection limit conclusions; do not treat uptake as proof of comfort.

SAVE.title: The Open Questions Board
SAVE.proposal:
Celebrate failed attempts by treating them as contributions to the café’s shared understanding of uncertainty. The mechanism is collective sense-making: an unresolved item can reveal a recurring question worth investigating, without putting its owner on display.

Before the event, volunteers turn permitted repair notes into three or four anonymous, non-procedural questions, such as “What information was missing before diagnosis?” or “When did we recognize that this repair exceeded our facilities?” Each card includes an honest statement of what remains unknown. Avoid item descriptions that could identify someone.

Visitors may silently read the board, place a pencil mark beside a question that helped them understand their own visit, or submit a new question on paper. Nothing requires describing their repair publicly. New submissions need a separate publication-consent tick and volunteer review. The closing ritual is a handwritten board footer: “These questions are worth carrying forward,” followed by one or two questions selected for relevance and safe scope, without vote totals or rankings. No promise of a future answer is made.

One volunteer prepares the initial cards, one checks proposed additions during quiet periods, and all four continue their ordinary repair roles. Reading and marking happen at the table edge after handback, outside the queue.

This assumes shared uncertainty can reduce isolation and support learning. It could instead resemble a catalogue of inadequacy or invite speculative technical advice. Keep all cards about observations, information needs, and service limits; omit repair instructions and unsupported explanations.
SAVE.experiment: Display the same permitted note summaries first as plain anonymous accounts and then as open questions, switching order midway through the event if practical. Offer separate optional paper responses: “What, if anything, did this help you understand?” and “Did this display make failed repairs feel more acceptable, unchanged, or more uncomfortable?” Observe congestion and whether visitors can bypass it easily. Compare the specificity of learning responses and reported discomfort between versions. The mechanism is doubtful if questions generate only vague approval, greater discomfort, or unsafe advice submissions. Different visitors and time periods make this a small design check, not causal proof.

SAVE.title: Thank the Care, Leave the Outcome
SAVE.proposal:
Use a private acknowledgment ritual to separate appreciation of a repair attempt from whether it succeeded. The mechanism is relational: a visitor can feel respected when someone recognizes a specific act of care, without having to reinterpret disappointment as success.

At handback, a volunteer may offer a folded paper card: “Would you like a short acknowledgment of the attempt? Passing is fine.” Inside, the volunteer writes one truthful, observable contribution, such as “You explained the fault clearly” or “We stopped when we reached the limits of our equipment.” Avoid praising persistence indiscriminately, assigning blame, or implying that stopping proves a repair was safe. The visitor can keep, decline, or discard it without explanation. There is no public reading.

A separate optional slip asks, “What care or effort would you like this café to recognize?” Visitors may acknowledge listening, patience, clear explanations, or respecting a decision to stop. With explicit permission, volunteers summarize these themes anonymously on the board under “Care we noticed today.” The board contains neither identifiable repair stories nor individual credits. This makes celebration visible while keeping personal acknowledgment private.

Four volunteers agree on a few factual wording examples before opening. Cards are completed only when handback allows; otherwise a visitor can take a blank reflection card to the table. One volunteer checks board contributions during a lull. Existing notes are unnecessary.

The approach assumes recognition feels supportive. It may seem patronizing, especially after a frustrating visit, and it does not itself establish technical learning. The offer must be brief, sincere, and easy to refuse.
SAVE.experiment: Compare ordinary handbacks with handbacks offering the private acknowledgment during alternating short periods. Give both groups optional anonymous exit questions: “I felt respected,” “I can name something learned or a limit clarified,” and “I felt expected to be positive,” each with yes/unsure/no options. Observe added handback time, repeated offers after refusal, and any queue obstruction. A useful result would combine respect with identifiable learning or clearer limits, without increased pressure. Reject or revise the ritual if appreciation rises but pressure also rises, or if visitors describe it as patronizing. Sparse feedback leaves uncertainty; silence and acceptance are not evidence of comfort.

SAVE.title: The Volunteers Go First
SAVE.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible so visitors encounter fallibility as an ordinary part of skilled work. The mechanism is modeling: people may feel less personally judged when helpers openly acknowledge their own uncertainty and mistakes.

Before opening, two volunteers each prepare a short, truthful account of an unsuccessful attempt involving their own belongings, or an account they have explicit permission to share anonymously. Each follows three prompts: “What I expected,” “What the attempt actually showed,” and “What I would notice earlier next time.” Include only supported observations, without repair procedures, identifying details, or claims that an unresolved item is safe.

Put these accounts on the small board under “Our attempts don’t always work either.” The monthly ritual is for volunteers to add one honest learning sentence before the doors open. Visitors can read silently or bypass the display; nobody asks them to contribute their own failure. A paper footer says, “Disappointment is welcome here too.” This celebrates helpers’ willingness to learn without requiring owners to feel grateful about a broken item.

Two volunteers supply accounts, a third checks accuracy and privacy, and the fourth checks that the display is readable from outside the queue. Preparation needs paper and a brief discussion; no volunteer remains stationed at the board.

This assumes volunteers can share credible examples without turning them into heroic stories. Self-deprecating jokes, exaggerated incompetence, or accounts that quietly blame owners could undermine trust. If suitable accounts are unavailable, do not invent them. Reading a display also cannot establish that visitors have learned anything transferable.
SAVE.experiment: For two short periods, show either the volunteer accounts or a plain explanation of the café’s repair limits, alternating their order once. Offer optional anonymous paper ticks about useful learning, embarrassment, and confidence in the helpers, plus an optional sentence naming something learned. One volunteer observes obstruction and checks that bypassing visitors receive no further invitation. Revise or reject the display if it increases discomfort or weakens confidence without producing specific learning. Small, self-selected responses cannot establish a reliable effect.

SAVE.title: The Next-Time Choice
SAVE.proposal:
Turn an unsuccessful attempt into a short opportunity to rehearse a useful decision. The mechanism is active application: visitors try using a lesson in a different situation, rather than merely reading that a lesson exists.

Using existing notes permitted for anonymous summarization, volunteers prepare two paper cases. Each describes an unsuccessful attempt and a documented information gap or service limit. Remove distinctive item details. Follow each case with a nontechnical choice, such as: “Before another visit, what would help most: record when the fault occurs, assume a cause, or leave the description blank?” Under a folded flap, explain why an observation could help while explicitly saying that it does not guarantee repair. Include “There isn’t enough information” wherever that is the honest answer.

The board reads “An attempt we can learn with.” The ritual is a silent choose-and-reveal moment at the table after handback. Visitors may point privately, think without marking anything, or skip it. Their own repair is never the exercise. There are no scores, correct-answer totals, prizes, or requests to demonstrate competence aloud.

One volunteer drafts the cases, another verifies that the lessons follow from the notes, a third checks for identifying details and unsafe implications, and the fourth places the materials away from the queue. All return to ordinary duties. Cards stay within observation, communication, and café boundaries; they contain no instructions for opening, powering, or testing equipment.

The prerequisite is at least one note with a defensible lesson. The limits are accessibility and tone: a quiz-like presentation could feel childish or evaluative. Use adult language, large writing, and an explicit invitation to ignore the exercise.
SAVE.experiment: Compare one folded choice case with a plain card containing the same case and explanation. Optional anonymous feedback asks visitors to apply the lesson to one different, equally safe example and report whether the format felt helpful, embarrassing, or like a test. Observe bypasses and table congestion without tracking individuals. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the choice version produces no clearer application than ordinary reading, or adds embarrassment. A few successful answers show feasibility, not lasting learning.

SAVE.title: One Attempt Changes the Café
SAVE.proposal:
Celebrate unsuccessful attempts through a small change to how the café works. The mechanism is institutional responsiveness: a failed repair becomes useful because the organization acts on a supported lesson, rather than asking its owner to supply a positive interpretation.

Before the event, review permitted repair notes for one recurring, nontechnical service issue that contributed to an unproductive attempt. Examples could include an unclear description of available facilities or a missed opportunity to ask when a fault occurs. Only choose an issue supported by the notes and a change achievable with paper during this event.

Write a three-part board card: “An attempt revealed…,” “Today we are trying…,” and “We still don’t know….” For example, an unsuccessful diagnosis might motivate an optional written prompt about when a problem appears. Do not imply that the change will make repairs succeed. Remove identifying details and omit unsafe repair advice.

The ritual is a short, quiet opening action: the volunteers place the revised prompt or clarification into use and turn the board card from “proposed” to “trying today.” Visitors can silently leave a paper comment or ignore the display. Contributions about personal experiences remain private unless separately approved for anonymous publication. No individual receives credit or blame.

The four volunteers divide note review, drafting, privacy checking, and observation, then resume their usual roles. The change must fit existing handbacks or optional paperwork rather than create another queue stage.

This assumes a modest service improvement is available and volunteers can implement it consistently. The board must not advertise a speculative improvement as an achieved result. A lesson may concern café organization rather than repair technique; that still counts, but should be described honestly.
SAVE.experiment: Try the revised prompt during one short period and use the ordinary process during another. Inspect whether the specific problem identified in the notes occurs less often, while recording approximate added time and optional anonymous learning and embarrassment ticks. Observe whether declined prompts are immediately dropped. Withdraw the change if it adds friction without addressing the problem, or makes visitors feel responsible for improving the café. Sparse observations support a local revision, not a claim that failed repairs generally improve services.

SAVE.title: Room for an Unfinished Ending
SAVE.proposal:
Reduce shame by changing the expectation visitors bring to a repair attempt. The mechanism is expectation calibration: an unresolved outcome may feel less like personal failure when it was presented beforehand as a legitimate possibility with its own useful forms of closure.

At the table, place a plain paper card headed “What today might provide.” Give equal visual space to three possibilities: “A repair,” “A clearer observation or limit,” and “Still unresolved.” Add: “You do not have to call an unsuccessful visit a success.” Visitors may read it silently; staff do not ask them to choose or predict an outcome.

At handback, use the ordinary factual explanation. An optional take-away strip repeats the three possibilities and says, “An unfinished attempt belongs here too.” The monthly celebration is a board heading, “We make room for unfinished work,” accompanied by one or two permitted anonymous examples showing different endings. Include an example where nothing clear was learned if the notes support one. Do not publish visitor names, photographs, identifiable cases, or new contributions without explicit consent.

One volunteer drafts the card, another checks that the examples accurately reflect the notes, a third checks privacy and safety, and the fourth checks placement outside the moving queue. No additional conversation or dedicated station is required.

This assumes some embarrassment comes from expecting every competent attempt to end in a repair. It will help less when distress comes from cost, attachment, or an unpleasant interaction. It could also sound like an excuse for poor service. Keep wording specific to uncertainty, maintain normal care, and avoid presenting every unsuccessful attempt as educational.
SAVE.experiment: During alternating arrival periods, display either this outcomes card or a similarly sized card explaining ordinary event logistics. Both periods receive the same optional anonymous exit questions: “Did your visit provide useful learning?”, “Did the outcome feel personally embarrassing?”, and “Did the café seem to excuse avoidable problems?” Observe queue movement and whether visitors can bypass all materials without follow-up. The approach is weakened if embarrassment stays unchanged, learning declines, or visitors perceive lowered standards. Differences between arrival groups and voluntary feedback leave substantial uncertainty.
